# Evaluating large language models for multilingual vulnerability detection at dual granularities

- Authors: Shu, Honglin; Fu, Michael; Yu, Junji; Wang, Dong; Tantithamthavorn, Chakkrit; Chen, Junjie; Kamei, Yasutaka
- Year / venue: 2026, Empirical Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1007/s10664-026-10832-4 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-026-10832-4
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

> Version note: the text analysed is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026, 53 pages, journal "manuscript No." template) (p. 1), not the typeset EMSE version. Page refs are PDF pages of this preprint.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Evaluate how well pre-trained code language models (PLMs) and large language models (LLMs) detect vulnerabilities across seven programming languages, at both function level and line level. Prior work focused on C/C++ and function-level detection (p. 1, p. 3, p. 4).
- [A] Working hypothesis: LLMs with suitable learning strategies (instruction tuning, few-shot prompting) improve multilingual function- and line-level detection (p. 4).
- [A] The paper extends the authors' ISSTA'25 workshop paper (Yu et al. 2025b) with embedding models, few-shot prompting and instruction tuning, line-level detection, CWE/severity analyses, and model size/reasoning experiments (p. 5).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: How effective are PLMs and LLMs at detecting multilingual vulnerabilities at function level? (p. 4)
- RQ2: ... at line level? (p. 4)
- RQ3: What are the strengths and weaknesses of PLMs and LLMs in multilingual detection? (p. 4)
- Discussion experiments: code-structure analysis, model size (70B), reasoning LLMs, time-split leakage check, imbalanced setting, deployment cost (p. 32-p. 43).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled empirical comparison on a fixed random 8:1:1 split, stratified by language, of the REEF dataset (p. 7, p. 8).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - PLMs (function level): CodeBERT, CodeT5, CodeT5P, UniXcoder and LineVul, fully fine-tuned with an MLP head on the [CLS] token. OpenAI Text-Embedding-Ada-002 / 3-Small / 3-Large are used as frozen encoders with a trained classifier head (p. 9, p. 16).
  - PLMs (line level): CodeBERT, UniXcoder, CodeT5, CodeT5P, with up to 113 lines x 31 tokens per function, GRU per line, per-line sigmoid, threshold 0.5. LineVul and the embedding models are excluded at line level (p. 22).
  - LLMs: DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B, Code Llama 7B, Llama 3 8B (HuggingFace), GPT-3.5-Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo-0125), GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) (p. 10, p. 15). Strategies: zero-shot; few-shot with 3 BM25-retrieved training examples; instruction tuning (LoRA) followed by zero-shot or few-shot prompting (p. 12, p. 14). GRACE (AST-enhanced LLM, zero-shot) is added as a baseline at function level (p. 10, p. 11).
  - Line-level LLM prompts state that the function is vulnerable, and lines are tagged "Line N:" (p. 11, p. 23).
  - Extra models: Code Llama 70B and Llama 3 70B (p. 35); reasoning LLMs DeepSeek-R1 (671B) and QwQ-plus, zero-shot only (p. 37).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: dummy classifiers that predict all-vulnerable or all-clean (p. 11). **No static-analysis (SAST) tool and no GNN/RNN detector is evaluated.** GNNs/RNNs are excluded because ASTs are language-specific and PLMs were previously shown to be better (p. 9, p. 10). MSIVD and Vul-RAG are excluded for lack of multilingual knowledge/explanations (p. 11).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): REEF (Wang et al. 2023a): 4,466 CVEs, 30,987 patches, NVD + Mend CVE list, 2016-2023, seven languages (p. 6).
- Sampling / selection method: comments removed; functions extracted with Tree-sitter; the pre-change function is labelled vulnerable and the post-change function clean (matched by name, then by edit distance); functions longer than 512 removed (PLM input limit) (p. 6). Line labels come from deleted lines (difflib); vulnerable functions fixed by additions only are dropped (p. 6, p. 7). Split: 8:1:1 stratified random sampling per language (p. 7, p. 8). "Exact-match filtering" against leakage (p. 44).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - Function level: 20,165 functions (10,133 vulnerable / 10,032 clean); train 16,126 / val 2,013 / test 2,026. Per language: C 3,056; C++ 1,792; C# 427; Go 2,905; Java 3,235; JavaScript 5,468; Python 3,282. Test sets per language: C 307, C++ 181, C# 44, Go 292, Java 325, JavaScript 548, Python 329 (p. 7, Table 1).
  - Line level: 8,134 vulnerable functions (train 6,513 / val 811 / test 810); 25,161 vulnerable vs 150,607 non-vulnerable lines. C# test set has only 13 functions (p. 8, Table 2).
  - Tree-sitter extraction check: 377 random samples, 93% / 92% judged correct by two authors, Cohen's kappa 0.9448 (p. 7).
  - Severity: 1.2% low, 41.12% high, 25.09% critical (CVSS v4.0) (p. 8).
  - Time-split set (2024-2025, same pipeline): 3,138 function-level samples (balanced) and 1,328 line-level samples (p. 38).
  - Imbalanced set (benign functions mined from unchanged functions): train 48,219 / val 6,012 / test 6,051; test = 1,019 vulnerable + 5,032 benign (p. 39).
- Data availability (public? link?): data, training and evaluation scripts on GitHub (SpanShu96/Large-Language-Model-for-Multilingual-Vulnerability-Detection) (p. 48).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: PLMs replicated following Steenhoek et al. 2024a, using the original authors' hyper-parameters (p. 15, p. 43). LoRA for instruction tuning (p. 14, p. 16). Hardware: Xeon Gold 6342, 512 GB RAM, 2 x A800 GPUs (p. 16). Detailed hyper-parameters (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank, temperature/decoding) are not reported in the paper; it refers to the replication package (p. 16). How GPT-3.5/GPT-4o were instruction-tuned is not described explicitly, but Table 12 lists per-token training costs for them (p. 41).
- Metrics are pooled over all test samples across languages, not averaged per language (p. 15).
- Code availability: yes (p. 48).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (binary), FPR, FNR, MCC, AUC (trapezoidal) (p. 14, p. 15). Accuracy is the primary metric at function level because the data is balanced; F1 is primary at line level because the data is imbalanced (p. 17, p. 23). RQ3 uses the share of correct detections per Top-25 CWE (2023 list) and per CVSS severity, plus Venn diagrams of unique correct/incorrect predictions (p. 27, p. 28).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): **none.** No significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs/seeds are reported. The words "significantly" and "significant" are used without tests (e.g. p. 21, p. 26, p. 38).

## 7. Key findings
1. Function level, balanced (Table 3): best LLM = GPT-4o with instruction tuning + few-shot (ITFSP): Acc 0.7196, P 0.7454, R 0.6722, F1 0.7069, FPR 0.2324, MCC 0.4360, AUC 0.7169. Best PLM = CodeT5P: Acc 0.6037, P 0.5626, R 0.9529, F1 0.7075, FPR 0.7496, MCC 0.2860, AUC 0.6015 — [V] (p. 17). F1 is essentially tied (0.7069 vs 0.7075); the gap is in accuracy/precision/FPR/MCC.
2. Every other LLM configuration at function level is near chance: zero-shot accuracy 0.4827-0.5061 (GRACE 0.5061), MCC −0.0585 to 0.0244; few-shot without tuning lowers accuracy for all but GPT-4o (e.g. GPT-3.5 0.3618, DeepSeek-Coder 0.3870); best instruction-tuned zero-shot is GPT-4o at 0.5874 — [V] (p. 17, p. 19).
3. Text-embedding models, CodeBERT and LineVul are near random at function level (Acc 0.5030-0.5173, AUC 0.50-0.51; LineVul and CodeBERT rows identical) — [V] (p. 17).
4. Per language, function level (Acc): GPT-4o ITFSP — C 0.7557, C# 0.7273, C++ 0.7901, Go 0.8082, JavaScript 0.6642, Java 0.7169, Python 0.6626. CodeT5P — C 0.5081, C# 0.6136, C++ 0.5249, Go 0.6062, JavaScript 0.7062, Java 0.6031, Python 0.5623 — [V] (p. 21). In JavaScript, CodeT5P (0.7062) and CodeT5 (0.6898) beat GPT-4o (0.6642). This contradicts the claim that GPT-4o "outperformed all other PLMs and LLMs across all seven studied languages" (p. 22) — [V] (p. 21, p. 22).
5. Line level (Table 4): GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.6641 (P 0.7012, R 0.6307, MCC 0.6563, AUC 0.8116) vs best PLM CodeT5P F1 0.4841 (P 0.3536, R 0.7673, MCC 0.5029, AUC 0.8644). GPT-4o few-shot without tuning already gives F1 0.6050. Zero-shot LLM F1 is 0.2254-0.3313 — [V] (p. 23, p. 25, p. 26). CodeT5P has the higher AUC — [V] (p. 26).
6. Per language, line level (F1): GPT-4o ITFSP — C 0.5478, C# 0.4348, C++ 0.5774, Go 0.7078, JavaScript 0.7815, Java 0.6391, Python 0.6055. CodeT5P — C 0.3727, C# 0.4750, C++ 0.4768, Go 0.4146, JavaScript 0.6556, Java 0.4167, Python 0.4519 — [V] (p. 26). CodeT5P wins in C# (13 test functions) — [V] (p. 8, p. 26).
7. Imbalanced function-level setting (~17% vulnerable; Table 11): the ranking reverses. Best F1 is UniXcoder 0.4626 (MCC 0.3495); CodeT5P has the highest MCC 0.3627; GPT-4o ITFSP reaches F1 0.4010, MCC 0.2774. The authors conclude the PLM "remains superior in overall classification balance" in the imbalanced setting — [V] (p. 40, p. 41). Instruction-tuned GPT-4o zero-shot has P 0.9659 but R 0.0834 — [V] (p. 40).
8. Top-25 CWEs (function level, per-CWE accuracy over vulnerable + clean functions, 1,119 test items): GPT-4o ITFSP 75.87% vs CodeT5P 61.13%. It is best on 23 of 25 CWEs (CodeT5P leads or ties on 7); e.g. CWE-787 82.93% vs 56.1%, CWE-79 78.28% vs 63.13%, CWE-89 78.26% vs 58.7% — [V] (p. 29, p. 30, Table 5).
9. Top-25 CWEs (line level, 441 items): GPT-4o ITFSP 50.79% vs CodeT5P 21.77%. Memory-safety CWEs are hardest: CWE-787 1/16 (6.25%), CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27% — [V] (p. 30, Table 6). The authors find 11 CWEs, including CWE-787, CWE-125 and CWE-22, are "detected" at function level but not at line level — [A] (p. 31).
10. Severity: at function level GPT-4o ITFSP has 630 correct High-severity detections vs CodeT5P 514, but fewer Critical (305 vs 321). At line level, 134 Critical vs 76 — [V] (p. 32).
11. Complementarity: CodeT5P has the most unique correct function-level detections (108 vs 28 for GPT-4o ITFSP), but GPT-4o ITFSP has the fewest unique incorrect detections (11 vs 136) — [V] (p. 29). In 608 LLM-only-correct vs 370 PLM-only-correct functions, the LLM-only set has higher median cyclomatic complexity (4.0 vs 2.0), tokens (135.5 vs 96.0) and LOC (19 vs 15), but lower nesting (2.0 vs 3.0) — [V] (p. 32, p. 34).
12. Model size: 70B Code Llama / Llama 3 bring no function-level gain (accuracies 0.4659-0.5093). At line level, Llama 3 70B few-shot F1 is 0.5214 vs 0.2822 for 8B, while Code Llama 70B gets worse (0.2267 vs 0.3257) — [V] (p. 35, p. 36).
13. Reasoning LLMs (zero-shot): DeepSeek-R1 Acc 0.5217 / line F1 0.2746; QwQ-plus Acc 0.5346 / line F1 0.3136. Only slightly above random, and not better than non-reasoning LLMs at line level — [V] (p. 37, p. 38).
14. Time-split check (2024-2025 CVEs): GPT-4o ITFSP function-level Acc 0.7874, F1 0.7804, MCC 0.5767; line-level F1 0.3450, MCC 0.3301 (down from 0.6641 in-distribution) — [V] (p. 38, p. 39, Table 10). The authors conclude the LLM "does not merely memorize" — [A] (p. 39).
15. Cost: GPT-4o instruction tuning $86.07 (function) / $59.42 (line); inference input ≈$1.65 / $0.95 for the test set. A local A6000 PLM training run costs ≈$5.59 (≈15x cheaper), with break-even after 58 fine-tuning runs — [V] (p. 41, p. 42). The authors recommend PLMs for organisations with privacy constraints or only consumer GPUs — [A] (p. 42, p. 43).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Only the REEF dataset and seven languages; generalisation to other languages is unknown (p. 43).
- [A] The 512-token limit of the PLMs restricts context for longer code (p. 43).
- [A] Single-language specialised LLM detectors (mostly C/C++) are excluded, which limits comparison with customised tools (p. 43).
- [A] Tree-sitter may misidentify functions (sanity check done) (p. 43).
- [A] Leakage from the same project/developer across splits is possible; only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44).
- [A] Tangled commits add label noise; heuristics reduce it, but line-level manual verification is future work (p. 44).
- [A] Reasoning LLMs were not fine-tuned with RL (p. 38).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **No static-analysis tool is compared.** For our RQ1, this paper supports only LLM-vs-DL/PLM claims, not LLM-vs-SAST. Based on §3 (p. 9-p. 11).
- [I] **The headline result rests on one configuration.** GPT-4o ITFSP is the only LLM setting clearly above chance at function level (next best 0.5874). Few-shot hurts every other model, and the paper gives no explanation, ablation, seed variation or test. A single strong outlier without variance estimates is fragile. Based on Table 3 (p. 17).
- [I] **Possible leakage via paired functions and BM25 retrieval.** The split is random at function level (p. 7), and each vulnerable function has its fixed twin labelled clean (p. 6). Twins and functions from the same CVE/project can fall on opposite sides of the split, and BM25 few-shot retrieval from the training set could then return a near-identical twin with the opposite label. Only exact-match filtering is applied (p. 44). This could favour the few-shot + fine-tuned setting. It is a hypothesis only; the paper gives no retrieval-overlap statistics. Counter-evidence: BM25 examples come from the "REEF training dataset" (p. 12), and the time-split run evaluates the model "trained on the original dataset" (p. 38). If the same 2016–2023 pool was used for retrieval, twins of the 2024–2025 test functions cannot be in it, yet function-level accuracy stays high (0.7874 ≥ 0.7196; Table 10, p. 39; p. 17). That argues against twin/BM25 leakage driving the function-level advantage. The line-level drop (0.6641 → 0.3450, p. 39) remains compatible with the hypothesis. The paper does not state the retrieval pool for the time-split run (p. 38), so this counter-evidence is conditional. Strength stays weak.
- [I] **Line-level accuracy/FPR are probably inflated by padding.** The DummyClf_vul precision on the line-level test set is 0.0267 (p. 23), i.e. 2.67% vulnerable lines. But Table 2 implies about 14.3% vulnerable lines (25,161 / 175,768) (p. 8). 810 test functions x 113 padded line slots ≈ 91,530 slots, and 2.67% of that ≈ 2,440 vulnerable lines, close to the ≈2,500 expected from the dataset average (3.1 per function). This suggests metrics are computed over padded 113-line slots. If so, accuracy (≈0.95-0.98) and FPR are inflated and not comparable to other papers. F1/precision/recall are less affected. Our arithmetic, unconfirmed by the authors.
- [I] The line-level task is easier than real use: only known-vulnerable functions are given, the LLM prompt says the function is vulnerable (p. 11), and only functions with deleted lines are kept (p. 7).
- [I] Short functions only: functions over 512 tokens are removed (p. 6), and median LOC in the divergent samples is 9-36 (p. 33). Scale effects (RQ4) are not tested.
- [I] The 2024-2025 time-split accuracy (0.7874) is higher than in-distribution (0.7196) (p. 39, p. 17). This is unusual and unexplained. Line-level F1 halves (0.6641 → 0.3450), which suggests that localisation does not generalise well over time (p. 39).
- [I] Text vs. table mismatches: CodeBERT Acc 0.5163 in the text vs 0.5173 in the table (p. 18 vs p. 17); GPT-3.5 zero-shot 0.4758 vs 0.4827 (p. 19 vs p. 17); UniXcoder MCC 0.3475 vs 0.3495 (p. 41 vs p. 40); GPT-4o imbalanced zero-shot F1 "0.1264" in the text vs 0.2036 in the table (p. 40). The model is called "GPT-4" in places (p. 21, p. 38). Minor issues, but signs of limited proofreading.
- [I] The per-CWE "correct detection" percentage mixes vulnerable and clean items. At line level, what counts as "correct" for a function is not defined (p. 29, p. 30).
- [I] Pooled metrics are dominated by JavaScript (548 of 2,026 function-level test items) (p. 7, p. 15). C# results rest on 44 / 13 test functions (p. 7, p. 8).

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): random function-level split, not split by CVE, project or time (p. 7); possible twin/BM25 leakage (§9); possible padding effect on line-level metrics (§9); PLMs are reproduced from original hyper-parameters, while LLM prompt templates differ across strategies (p. 11, p. 13, p. 43).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): REEF only; seven languages; short functions (≤512 tokens) (p. 6, p. 43); balanced test (50/50) by default (p. 7). The imbalanced variant (p. 39) changes the conclusion.
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the line-level task presupposes a known-vulnerable function (p. 11). Labels come from fix commits (pre-change = vulnerable, post-change = clean) with known tangling noise (p. 6, p. 44). The authors report that two raters judged 92-93% of 377 extracted functions correct (p. 7).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests, confidence intervals or seeds. Many configurations (≈30) are compared on one split, and the best is chosen post hoc. Per-language and per-CWE cells are small (e.g. C# 44/13; CWE-862 n = 1) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 30).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): data and scripts are released (p. 48), and model versions are given for the OpenAI models (p. 15). Hyper-parameters, decoding settings and GPT fine-tuning details are not in the paper (p. 16).
- Funding: Chinese and Japanese public grants; no conflict of interest declared (p. 48).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: larger multilingual benchmarks; intermediate representations that unify code across languages; better PLM/LLM learning strategies such as multi-task learning or meta-learning to close the gap between high- and low-resource languages (p. 47); RL fine-tuning of reasoning LLMs (p. 38); line-level manual verification of labels (p. 44); adding specialised models as they support more languages (p. 43).
- Suggested by us [I]: add SAST baselines (CodeQL/Semgrep) on the same multilingual test split; split by CVE/project/time; repeat the GPT-4o ITFSP run with several seeds and BM25-overlap controls; compute line-level metrics on real lines only; evaluate realistic class ratios as the main setting.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM vs DL/PLM head-to-head; no SAST), RQ2 (balanced vs imbalanced reversal; time split; pooled metrics; line-level setup), RQ3 (cost/TCO of API LLM vs local PLM; no hybrid), RQ4 (per-language, per-CWE, per-severity, function complexity), RQ5 (leakage, granularity, imbalance).
- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few multilingual, two-granularity LLM-vs-PLM comparisons. Its main lesson for the review is conditional: only a fine-tuned frontier LLM with retrieved examples beats fine-tuned PLMs, and only on balanced data. Under realistic imbalance, fine-tuned PLMs match or beat it. Prompt-only LLMs are near chance at function level. This supports a "results depend on setup" answer to RQ2.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | On balanced REEF (7 languages), fine-tuned GPT-4o + BM25 few-shot beats best PLM CodeT5P at function level (Acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037; MCC 0.4360 vs 0.2860; F1 tied 0.7069 vs 0.7075) | p. 17 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Prompt-only LLMs (zero-/few-shot, incl. GPT-4o, GRACE, DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-plus) are near chance at function level (Acc 0.36-0.53, MCC ≤0.07) | p. 17, p. 37 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Line level: GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.6641 vs CodeT5P 0.4841 (but CodeT5P AUC 0.8644 > 0.8116) | p. 23, p. 26 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Under realistic imbalance (~17% vulnerable), PLMs outperform the best LLM (UniXcoder F1 0.4626 / CodeT5P MCC 0.3627 vs GPT-4o ITFSP F1 0.4010 / MCC 0.2774) — conclusion flips with class ratio | p. 40, p. 41 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Time-split (2024-2025) GPT-4o ITFSP keeps function-level Acc 0.7874 but line-level F1 drops to 0.3450 from 0.6641 | p. 39 | V | moderate |

Counter-evidence: time-split function-level Acc stays 0.7874 (retrieval pool for that run not stated); line-level drop to 0.3450 still compatible | p. 6, p. 7, p. 12, p. 38–39, p. 44 | I | weak |
| RQ2 | Line-level dummy precision 0.0267 vs ~14% vulnerable lines in dataset suggests metrics over padded 113-line slots, inflating accuracy/FPR | p. 8, p. 22, p. 23 | I | weak |
| RQ3 | GPT-4o instruction tuning costs $86.07 (function) vs ≈$5.59 per local A6000 PLM training run (~15x cheaper); authors recommend PLMs under privacy/limited hardware | p. 42 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | GPT-4o ITFSP per-language function Acc: Go 0.8082 (best) to Python 0.6626 (worst); CodeT5P beats it in JavaScript (0.7062 vs 0.6642) | p. 21 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Line-level F1 by language: JavaScript 0.7815 best, C# 0.4348 worst (CodeT5P better in C#, n = 13) | p. 8, p. 26 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | Memory-safety CWEs are hardest to localise: line-level correct rate CWE-787 6.25%, CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27% (best model) | p. 30 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | LLM-only correct functions are more complex/longer (median CC 4.0 vs 2.0; 135.5 vs 96 tokens) than PLM-only correct ones; PLM handles deeper nesting | p. 34 | V | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "GPT-4o with instruction tuning and few-shot prompting demonstrates superior performance, achieving the highest accuracy (0.7196) at function-level compared to the best-performing CodeT5P (0.6037)" (p. 4)

> "the PLM remains superior in overall classification balance for this imbalanced dataset." (p. 41)

> "the size of LLMs is not the decisive factor affecting performance on multilingual vulnerability detection, and the use of reasoning LLMs does not lead to significant improvements." (p. 4)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: pp. 1-48 read in full (all sections, tables 1-12, threats, conclusion, declarations). The reference list (pp. 48-53) was skimmed. Figures 4, 5 and 8-10 are bar charts garbled by text extraction; we rely on the numbers the authors give in the text for them (p. 21, p. 26, p. 32, p. 34).
- Version: metadata = EMSE 2026 (DOI 10.1007/s10664-026-10832-4). The analysed text is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026), identity matched by arXiv id. The typeset journal version may differ slightly. The running header reads "W. Dong et al.", a template artifact.
- Uncertainties: (1) The padding hypothesis and the twin/BM25 leakage hypothesis (§9) are our inference from reported numbers; the replication package could settle both. (2) How GPT-3.5/GPT-4o were instruction-tuned (OpenAI fine-tuning API vs. other) is not stated; we infer the API from the Table 12 training costs (p. 41). (3) "Break-even after 58 runs" (p. 42) is reproducible as $4,650 / ($86.07 − $5.59) ≈ 57.8. It assumes a fresh GPU purchase and ignores PLM inference and engineering cost.

# A Systematic Literature Review on Detecting Software Vulnerabilities with Large Language Models

- Authors: Kaniewski, Sabrina; Schmidt, Fabian; Enzweiler, Markus; Menth, Michael; Heer, Tobias
- Year / venue: 2026, ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3815425 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3815425
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
- **Version analysed:** arXiv:2507.22659v2 (19 Dec 2025) (p. 1), the preprint of the TOSEM article (DOI 10.1145/3815425), not the typeset journal version. Study statistics are "as of December 13th 2025" (p. 8).

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Convention for this survey: two kinds of numbers are marked [V]: counts about the review's own corpus shown in its own tables and figures, and dataset statistics that the authors recomputed from the published datasets (Table 5 states the numbers "are reproduced with the officially published datasets", p. 28). They are the review's own data, although we cannot re-check the extraction. Anything reported about results of individual primary studies is second-hand and marked [A], never [V].

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Map the fragmented field of LLM-based software vulnerability detection. The authors argue that studies are hard to compare because of different system designs, datasets, metrics and splits (p. 1–2).
- [A] Contributions (p. 2–3):
  - an SLR of 263 studies (Jan 2020–Nov 2025)
  - a taxonomy covering task formulation, input representation, system architecture, adaptation/orchestration technique and dataset usage
  - an in-depth dataset analysis (class balance, CWE coverage/diversity)
  - limitations and future directions
  - a living public repository (Awesome-LLM4SVD)
- [A] The term "LLM" is used broadly and includes small pre-trained models such as BERT and CodeBERT (footnote, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: How is the detection task formulated in LLM-based systems? (p. 6)
- RQ2: How are input and vulnerability semantics represented for LLMs? (p. 6)
- RQ3: What are the predominant techniques for adapting LLMs to detection? (p. 6)
- RQ4: Which datasets are used, and how does dataset selection affect applicability? (p. 6)
- RQ5: How does dataset selection affect comparability across studies? (p. 6)
- No hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: SLR following Kitchenham et al. guidelines (p. 5). It has three phases: literature search, study selection and study analysis (Fig. 1, p. 8).
- Search: automated search of IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library and arXiv on titles/abstracts (p. 6–7). The full Boolean search string is printed: LLM/model-family terms AND (vulnerability/CVE/CWE) AND (detect*/identif*/classif*/analy*/discover*/assess*) AND (software/program/code) (p. 7). The initial search ran in December 2024, followed by continuous database alerts and scholar.inbox notifications (p. 7).
- Inclusion criteria [A]: title or abstract matches the search string; the study uses **and evaluates** LLMs for software vulnerability detection and introduces novel techniques or systems (Table 2, p. 8).
- Exclusion criteria [A] (Table 2, p. 8; p. 7):
  - not in English, or full text not accessible
  - reviews, surveys, theses, abstracts, posters, demos, tutorials
  - binary code, smart contracts, network analysis or malware
  - studies that use LLMs **only to work on outputs of other tools (e.g. SAST)**
  - LLMs mentioned only in passing or used merely as baselines
  - duplicates or extended versions
- Quality assessment [A]: a manual check of contribution, workflow/implementation description, evaluation setup (datasets, baselines, metrics) and coherence of findings, motivated by the inclusion of preprints (p. 7). The scoring scheme, threshold and number of excluded studies are not reported.
- Snowballing: backward (reference lists) and forward (Google Scholar citations), with snowballed studies passing the same criteria (p. 7).
- Extraction: task definition, LLMs used, adaptation techniques, input representation, datasets, targeted CWEs and metrics (p. 7–8).
- Number of reviewers, independent double screening and inter-rater agreement: not reported.
- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable. The review does **not** synthesise LLM-vs-SAST or LLM-vs-DL performance. Studies that use LLMs only as baselines are excluded (p. 8).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): ACM DL (514 hits), IEEE Xplore (865), arXiv (2,776) [V] (Fig. 1, p. 8). Screening counts per stage (title/abstract, full text, quality, snowballing) are not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: 263 primary studies [V] (p. 7–8): 185 peer-reviewed and 78 (29.7%) arXiv preprints [V] (p. 8; Fig. 2, p. 9). The earliest study is from 2020 (p. 8). The A*/A conference and Q1 journal venues are listed in Table 3, e.g. ICSE 13 and TSE 7 [V] (p. 9).
- Time window: January 2020 – November 2025 (p. 1–2).
- Dataset analysis: 20 datasets are characterised (the 15 most used plus 5 selected recent ones; Tables 4–5, p. 26, p. 28). 12 real-world/mixed multi-class datasets are analysed for CWE distribution, with D2A and FormAI excluded (p. 30).
- Data availability: artifacts and the categorised study list are in a public GitHub repository [144] (p. 3, p. 43).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, tools: full-text review with structured extraction (p. 7–8). The taxonomy categories are refined iteratively and aligned with existing definitions where possible (p. 43). CWE clustering uses the MITRE CWE-1000 Research View pillars (p. 30–32). Dataset usage is analysed over time (Fig. 11, p. 34), by co-usage pairs (Fig. 12, p. 35) and by overlap within use cases (Fig. 13, p. 36).
- Code availability: artifacts released [144] (p. 3).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - Study counts per taxonomy node, used to show prevalence.
  - Dataset size, % vulnerable samples and number of distinct CWEs, as proxies for label diversity and balance (p. 25, p. 28).
  - Share of CWE labels per CWE-1000 pillar and Top-25 CWE concentration, measuring thematic diversity (p. 31–32).
  - Dataset usage frequency and overlap, measuring comparability (p. 34–37).
- The review does not extract or pool the effectiveness metrics (precision/recall/F1) of primary studies, although "evaluation metrics" is listed among the extracted fields (p. 8).
- Statistical testing: none; not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Task formulation: binary classification dominates (195 studies). Vulnerability-specific classification: 20; multi-class: 61; multi-label: 23. Only a minority combine classification with generation tasks (description, root-cause reasoning, structured report) — [V] (p. 11; Fig. 4, p. 12)
2. Input: 139 studies feed raw code. Structured inputs (AST/CFG/DFG/PDG/CPG, slices, code gadgets) and auxiliary information (CWE lists, few-shot examples, execution context, SAST tool output) are used less often — [V] (p. 13–14)
3. Architecture and scale: decoder-only LLMs dominate. Tiny/small models (< 8B) are mostly full-parameter fine-tuned, while medium/large models are mostly prompted or PEFT-tuned. Hybrid LLM + GNN/RNN/CNN architectures form a distinct group — [V] (p. 15–16; Fig. 5, p. 16)
4. Advanced techniques are emerging but rare: RAG in 25 studies, LoRA in 27, agentic systems in 10, GNN hybrids in 20 — [V] (p. 36–37)
5. Dataset usage is concentrated on old function-level C/C++ benchmarks. Devign is used in 69 studies, Big-Vul in 63, ReVeal in 40, SARD in 32, DiverseVul and PrimeVul in 27 each — [V] (Table 4, p. 26)
6. Datasets are highly imbalanced. Recomputed vulnerable shares: Big-Vul 4.5%, DiverseVul 5.7%, PrimeVul 2.9%, D2A 1.4%, ReposVul 0.7%, compared with Devign 48.0% — [V] (Table 5, p. 28)
7. Real-world datasets follow a long-tail CWE distribution: the Top-25 CWEs account for about 80% of labels. Memory/resource-lifetime CWEs dominate, and several CWE-1000 pillars are absent from the Top 25 — [V] (p. 30, p. 32; Figs. 8–10)
8. 555 CWEs that are allowed for vulnerability mapping in CWE-1000 appear in none of the analysed datasets. Many dataset labels use discouraged or abstract CWEs (e.g. CWE-119, CWE-399, CWE-20) — [V] (p. 32, p. 34)
9. Fragmentation of evaluation setups:
   - 87 studies use or introduce custom datasets, and only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies (p. 35).
   - Few datasets have predefined train/validation/test splits: Draper, CodeXGLUE-Devign, Big-Vul, PrimeVul (p. 39).
   - Among agentic studies, only 4 of 10 share PrimeVul (p. 37).

   — [V] for the counts, [A] for the conclusion that cross-study comparison is unreliable
10. Data leakage: widely used static benchmarks (Devign, Big-Vul) are likely in LLM pre-training corpora, so high scores may reflect memorisation rather than generalisation — [A] (p. 30, p. 38–39)
11. Robustness: models rely on superficial textual patterns, and performance degrades under semantics-preserving transformations (renaming, reordering, formatting) — [A] (p. 39)
12. Practical deployment: there are few evaluations in realistic development settings, models often underperform outside curated benchmarks (citing our `chakraborty2024revisiting`), and costs are high — [A] (p. 39–40)
13. LLM–SAST relationship. LLMs are presented as free of the hand-written, language-specific rules that SAST needs (p. 1, p. 12–13). In the corpus, SAST appears as auxiliary input to LLMs: tool output in prompts, or hybrid workflows where the LLM verifies or refines static-analysis findings ([18], [145], [219], [340], [365]) (p. 14, p. 18). The authors see synergy of LLMs with program analysis as "a current pathway for industrial adoption": SAST detects and the LLM filters false positives, or the LLM proposes and static analysis verifies (p. 42). This is qualitative only, with no quantified comparison — [A]

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Paper retrieval omissions (keywords, a static snapshot of a living field), mitigated by a broad search string, snowballing, continuous alerts and a maintained repository (p. 42–43).
- [A] Study selection bias, including the decision not to filter by venue rank and to include preprints. Mitigated by reporting venue tiers and a manual quality assessment (p. 43).
- [A] Subjectivity in data extraction and taxonomy classification (e.g. "reasoning" vs "description"). Mitigated by aligning with existing definitions and releasing the categorised study list (p. 43).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] It is a mapping study, not an effectiveness synthesis. No precision/recall/F1 or false-positive data are pooled or compared, so it cannot answer RQ1 directly. Its value for us is RQ2/RQ5. Based on sections 4–6 and the absence of any results tables.
- [I] Scope excludes much of the hybrid design space we care about. Studies that use LLMs only to post-process SAST output (e.g. false-positive filtering) are excluded (p. 7–8). The very hybrid that the authors recommend for industry (p. 42) is therefore out of the corpus. Our RQ3 needs primary studies such as `du2026reducing`, `xiong2026sifting` and `li2024iris`.
- [I] Only three databases are searched (IEEE, ACM, arXiv) (p. 6). Springer, Elsevier, Wiley and USENIX/NDSS are not searched directly, which partly explains the high arXiv hit count. Snowballing and alerts mitigate this only partly.
- [I] Opaque quality assessment and screening. The QA criteria are listed without a scoring scheme or threshold, and per-stage exclusion counts, number of reviewers and agreement are not reported (p. 7–8). This is weaker than `zhou2025large`'s explicit 0–3 scoring.
- [I] The broad LLM definition (BERT/CodeBERT counted as LLMs, p. 2) and the inclusion of feature-extraction-only uses (p. 17) blur the line between "LLM-based" and "pre-trained-transformer DL" detectors. That line matters for our three-way LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison.
- [I] Minor internal inconsistencies:
  - The Fig. 11 caption says "Jan 2020 to Mar 2025" while the text says Jan 2020 to Nov 2025 (p. 34).
  - SecurityEval is described with "75 CWE types" (p. 29) but 69 CWEs in Table 5 (p. 28) and on p. 30.
  - Ding et al. (PrimeVul) appears twice in the references, as [54] (arXiv) and [55] (ICSE) (p. 46).
  - The statement that large models "achieve state-of-the-art performance on vulnerability detection benchmarks" (p. 15) has no citation.

  None of these affects the main conclusions.
- [I] Preprint-heavy corpus: 29.7% of studies are arXiv preprints (p. 8). Corpus-level counts mix peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed work, and the counts are not split by peer-review status.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): selection is subjective and the screening reliability is not reported. The exclusion of "LLM on tool output" studies shapes conclusions about hybrids (p. 7). The review itself highlights data leakage as a key threat in primary studies (p. 24, p. 30, p. 38–39).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): source code only, with binaries, smart contracts and malware excluded (p. 8). The corpus is C/C++-heavy because the datasets are (p. 28, p. 37).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the number of distinct CWEs is used as a proxy for label diversity (p. 25), and pillar mapping depends on the quality of NVD labels (p. 32). Counts of studies per technique measure popularity, not effectiveness.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable (no inferential analysis).
- Reproducibility: strong for an SLR. The full search string is printed (p. 7), and the artifacts and categorised studies are public [144] (p. 3, p. 43). Screening records and QA scores are not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (Table 7, p. 38; p. 40–42):
  - L1 Granularity: project- and repository-level detection; richer code context (callees, types, globals, execution/data flow); languages beyond C/C++ (Python, Java, Rust); multilingual and cross-project benchmarks (p. 40).
  - L2 Labels and quality: manual verification and better VFC labelling tools; reasoning-oriented benchmarks with verified root-cause explanations; datasets built after model knowledge cutoffs to avoid leakage; covering the 555 unused mappable CWEs (p. 40–41).
  - L3 Comparability: datasets with documented splits (or closed test sets); evaluating on multiple datasets (recent PrimeVul/MegaVul plus established Devign/Big-Vul); documenting all preprocessing; open science (p. 41).
  - L4 Up-to-date knowledge: automatically updated datasets (e.g. CVEfixes); RAG and continual learning (p. 41).
  - L5 Representation: structure-aware and language-agnostic inputs; LLM + GNN hybrids; robustness tests on perturbed or LLM-generated code (p. 41).
  - L6 Explainability: metrics for explanation trustworthiness; structured explanations (propagation paths); grounding via CWE hierarchies (p. 42).
  - L7 Integration (p. 42):
    - IDE/CI integration, field studies and evaluation on proprietary code
    - CWE-type classifiers
    - agentic self-assessment
    - SAST + LLM synergy in both directions (SAST then LLM false-positive filter; LLM then static-analysis verification)
    - model compression and on-premise small models
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - No direction asks for controlled, same-benchmark comparisons of LLMs against SAST tools and non-LLM DL detectors. This gap is consistent with `zhou2025large` and `sheng2025llms`, and is a candidate for our RQ5 gap section (requires a novelty check).
  - The recommended SAST + LLM pipelines (p. 42) are, by construction, outside this SLR's corpus. Evidence for them must come from studies this SLR excludes.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (strongest: dataset taxonomy, imbalance, CWE coverage, leakage, splits, fragmentation), RQ5 (L1–L7 limitations and directions), RQ4 (C/C++ bias, CWE long tail, missing pillars), RQ3 (qualitative: SAST output as LLM input; recommended hybrids). RQ1 is not answered.
- How it informs our work [I]: the most recent and largest SLR in our corpus (263 studies, to Nov 2025) and peer-reviewed (TOSEM). Its dataset analysis gives concrete, recomputed evidence for why reported numbers disagree across studies. That is the core of our RQ2: different benchmarks, extreme class-balance differences (0.7–100% vulnerable across Table 5; 1.4–50% among the function-level C/C++ benchmarks, p. 28), long-tailed CWE coverage, missing splits, custom datasets and leakage. It supports the claim that head-to-head LLM-vs-SAST/DL evidence must be read benchmark by benchmark.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | This 263-study SLR does not synthesise effectiveness; it presents SAST tools as rule-dependent with high false-positive rates, and LLMs as rule-free but unproven outside curated benchmarks (no pooled comparison) | 1, 12–13, 40 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | Most-used benchmarks are old function-level C/C++ datasets (Devign 69, Big-Vul 63, ReVeal 40 studies) with vulnerable shares from 0.7% (ReposVul) to 100% (SecurityEval) across Table 5, or 1.4% (D2A) to 50.0% (PairVul) among the function-level C/C++ benchmarks | 26, 28 | V | strong |
| RQ2 | 87 studies use or introduce custom datasets, only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies, and few datasets have predefined splits, so cross-study comparison is unreliable | 35, 39 | V | strong |
| RQ2 | Widely used benchmarks are likely in LLM pre-training corpora (data leakage), so high scores may reflect memorisation | 30, 38–39 | A | moderate |
| RQ3 | In LLM-based detectors, SAST output is used as auxiliary input, or the LLM verifies/refines static-analysis findings; studies that only post-process tool output are excluded from the SLR | 7–8, 14, 18 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Authors recommend SAST + LLM synergy (SAST detects then LLM filters false positives; LLM proposes then static analysis verifies) as a pathway to industrial adoption; not quantified | 42 | A | weak |
| RQ4 | Datasets are C/C++-biased and long-tailed (Top-25 CWEs ≈80% of labels); 555 mappable CWEs are absent from all analysed datasets; logic/interaction pillars are under-represented | 28, 32, 34 | V | strong |
| RQ5 | Seven open limitation themes: granularity, label quality/leakage, comparability, outdated knowledge, representation robustness, explainability, workflow integration/cost | 37–40 | A | moderate |
| RQ5 | Few studies evaluate in realistic development settings; models often underperform outside curated benchmarks | 39–40 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "studies frequently adopt custom datasets, metrics, and data splits, making it difficult to assess progress, reproduce results, or compare models fairly" (p. 2)

> "Only nine datasets are reused in more than ten studies, highlighting the lack of a standardized suite of benchmark datasets" (p. 35)

> "Pipelines where SAST tools detect candidates and LLMs filter false positives can significantly reduce alert fatigue" (p. 42)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage:
  - All 43 body pages read: methodology, taxonomy (sections 4.1–4.4), datasets (section 5), limitations and road ahead (section 6), threats, conclusion.
  - Long citation lists inside the taxonomy sections were skimmed, not checked individually.
  - The reference list (p. 44–63) was consulted for refs [29], [42], [54]/[55], [145], [159], [172], [219], [304], [368] and [394].
  - Figures 4, 5 and 8–13 are partly garbled in the text layer, so counts were taken from the running text and from Tables 4–5.

It also cites a separate LLM-vs-traditional-methods survey (Taghavi Far & Feyzi 2025, [304]) that is not in our project. That survey might be worth screening for RQ1.
- Funding / conflict of interest: DFG project 528745080 (p. 44). The first author's prior survey ([143]) seeded the search terms (p. 7).
- Uncertainties: per-stage screening numbers are unknown, and the quality-assessment threshold is unknown.

# LLMs in Software Security: A Survey of Vulnerability Detection Techniques and Insights

- Authors: Sheng, Ze; Chen, Zhicheng; Gu, Shuning; Huang, Heqing; Gu, Guofei; Huang, Jeff
- Year / venue: 2025, ACM Computing Surveys (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3769082 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3769082
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
- **Version analysed:** arXiv:2502.07049v2 (12 Feb 2025) (p. 1). This is the preprint of the ACM Computing Surveys article, not the typeset CSUR version. `kaniewski2026systematic` lists the published version as Sep 2025 with a 2017–2025 time frame (p. 4 of that paper), so the published content may differ from what is analysed here.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Convention for this survey: counts about the survey's own corpus that appear in its own tables, figures or "Finding" boxes are marked [V]. They are the survey's own data, although we cannot re-check the underlying extraction. Anything reported about results of individual primary studies (F1 scores, accuracies) is second-hand and marked [A], never [V].

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Survey the use of LLMs for software vulnerability detection: problem formulation, model selection, techniques, datasets, metrics, challenges and research directions (p. 1).
- [A] Claims to be "the first comprehensive survey" on strengths and weaknesses of LLMs in vulnerability detection (p. 2). It nevertheless acknowledges `zhou2025large` as prior work and differentiates itself by newer models (GPT-4o, o1, Claude 3.5 Sonnet), benchmark/metric analysis and detection-specific detail (p. 5).
- [A] Motivation: traditional static and dynamic analysis tools suffer from high false-positive rates, low efficiency and heavy effort across many vulnerability types (p. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: What LLMs have been applied to vulnerability detection? (p. 2)
- RQ2: What benchmarks, datasets and metrics have been designed to evaluate vulnerability detection? (p. 3)
- RQ3: What techniques have been used in LLMs for vulnerability detection? (p. 3)
- RQ4: What challenges do LLMs face in detecting vulnerabilities, and what are potential directions? (p. 3)
- No hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: narrative survey with a keyword-driven, iterative selection. It is **not** a protocol-based systematic review: no SLR guideline is cited, there is no search string or database list, no formal inclusion/exclusion table and no quality assessment (p. 3–4). `kaniewski2026systematic` also classifies it as non-SLR (✗) (p. 4 of that paper).
- Approach: started from top-tier security venues (S&P, USENIX Security, CCS) and journals such as IEEE TSE. Then searched with key terms ("vulnerability detection", "LLM", "large language model", "AI"), repeated every three weeks over two months (p. 3–4).
- Inclusion/exclusion [A]: in scope are LLM-based vulnerability detection studies, primarily on C/C++, Java and Solidity. Excluded are studies using traditional ML (CNN, RNN, LSTM) and studies unrelated to vulnerability detection, such as malware analysis or network intrusion detection (p. 3–4).
- Quality assessment: not reported (none described).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable. The survey does not compare LLMs with SAST or DL detectors, and it explicitly excludes traditional ML/DL approaches (p. 3).
- Number of reviewers, screening procedure, agreement: not reported.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): top security/SE venues plus keyword searches (p. 3–4). The databases used are not reported.
- Sample size (N) and unit: 58 "highly related" studies, within "more than 80 papers" selected from "over 500" screened (p. 3), or "approximately 500-600" screened (p. 4) [A]. The language statistics are based on "56 selected papers" (p. 10), not 58.
- Time window: 2019–2024 (p. 3). NVD CVE statistics were collected until 3 November 2024 (Table 3, p. 10).
- Sampling / selection method: iterative keyword search, see section 3. Preprints are included: the authors estimate that about 60% of research in the area appears as arXiv preprints (p. 26). The share of preprints in their own corpus is not reported.
- Data availability: a GitHub list of papers is maintained (p. 1). An extraction sheet is not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, tools: data extraction fields are not reported. The analysis is organised by RQ, with "Finding" boxes I–IX (p. 11–25).
- Code availability: not applicable; a paper list is on GitHub (p. 1).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: the survey uses counts and shares of models, languages and techniques. It also catalogues the metrics used by primary studies: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and MCC for imbalanced data; BLEU and ROUGE for generated descriptions; execution time for efficiency (p. 14). Table 5 lists one F1 score per fine-tuning study, each on a different dataset (p. 18).
- Statistical testing: none; not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Language focus of studies: C/C++ 50%, Java 21.1%, Solidity 11.8%, other (Python, PHP, Go) 16.6% — [V] (Finding I, p. 11)
2. Model usage: 33 distinct LLMs across 58 studies; GPT-4 is the most used (29 instances), then GPT-3.5 (25). By architecture: encoder-only 24.2%, encoder-decoder 8.7%, decoder-only 67.1% of usage — [V] (p. 8–9)
3. Datasets: 42 datasets are catalogued, mostly function- or file-level and C/C++. C/C++ accounts for about 60% of dataset coverage, and repository-level datasets are scarce. Only MAGMA and CWE-Bench-Java are repository-level (Table 4, p. 13; Finding II, p. 13) — [V]
4. About 40 studies (stated as 83%) analyse isolated code snippets. The authors argue that LLM performance on snippets exceeds what is seen in real-world detection ([37]) — [A] (p. 20)
5. LLMs and static analysis: for full-codebase analysis, "LLMs typically assist static analysis tools or support fuzzing tasks" rather than performing standalone analysis. Commit-level methods combine commits with static analysis results — [A] (p. 20)
6. Neuro-symbolic approaches (e.g. CodeQL or Bear combined with LLMs) "have shown promise on large-scale projects", but they still need better taint propagation modelling, more efficient LLM reasoning and cross-language adaptation — [A] (p. 3)
7. 41.3% of studies use code-processing techniques (AST/CFG/DFG, RAG, slicing). Gains over direct prompting are "modest" and shrink for complex cross-file vulnerabilities. Larger models' own gains "tend to outweigh" these preprocessing gains — [V] for the share / [A] for the interpretation (Finding III, p. 16)
8. Benchmark sensitivity, second-hand: Ding et al. (our `ding2025vulnerability`) report F1 of only 0.21 on PrimeVul. Guo et al. report CodeBERT at 0.099 F1 on PrimeVul but 0.66 on Choi2017. Table 5 reports F1 of 0.21–0.99 across different datasets — [A] (p. 18–19)
9. Vulnerability-type imbalance: memory-related vulnerabilities reach higher detection accuracy, while logic vulnerabilities are under-explored. One cited study reports high accuracy on CWE-787 but poor accuracy on CWE-862 — [A] (p. 3, p. 22)
10. LLMs detect vulnerabilities well in simple synthetic single functions, even zero-shot, but need much more context for larger projects. Callee functions may rely on their callers for protection, which causes wrong conclusions when they are analysed in isolation — [A] (p. 22)
11. LLMs lack robustness to perturbations and give inconsistent, run-to-run variable explanations, even when the detection itself is correct — [A] (p. 23)
12. Key challenges listed for LLM detection: data leakage that inflates metrics, understanding complex context, positional bias in long contexts, and high false-positive rates with poor zero-day performance — [A] (p. 14)

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Comprehensiveness: about 60% of the research appears only as arXiv preprints, and terminology variation may cause missed papers. Mitigation: keywords were extracted from published papers, and selection was refined over two months (p. 26).
- [A] Future versions will add localisation, assessment and patching tasks (p. 26).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Weak review methodology. There is no search string, no database list, no formal criteria, no quality appraisal and no PRISMA-style counts (p. 3–4). Its corpus-level statistics are therefore less reliable than those of a protocol-based SLR such as `kaniewski2026systematic`, and the survey should be weighted lower for "state of the field" claims.
- [I] Internal numeric inconsistencies, all from the text:
  - 58 studies (p. 8) vs 56 papers used for the language statistics (p. 10).
  - "approximately 40 studies (83%)" (p. 20) implies a denominator of about 48, not 58.
  - Minimum fine-tuning dataset size is "at least 10K samples" (p. 19) vs "at least 100,000 examples" (p. 24).
  - Encoder models are said to "dominate non-fine-tuning studies (72.4%)" (p. 10), while decoder-only models are 67.1% of overall usage and GPT-4/GPT-3.5 top the usage table (p. 9). With only about 30% of studies fine-tuning (p. 19), these figures are hard to reconcile.
- [I] Metric definition error: precision is described as the "true positive rate" (p. 14). True positive rate is recall. This is minor but signals limited editorial checking.
- [I] Possible citation mismatch: the CWE-787 vs CWE-862 performance contrast is attributed to [36] (p. 22). In the reference list, [36] is a 2021 repair paper ("Beyond Tests: Program Vulnerability Repair via Crash Constraint Extraction", p. 28). The intended source is probably [37] (Gao et al. 2023, "How far have we gone in vulnerability detection using large language models"), but this is unverified. Do not reuse this claim without checking the primary source.
- [I] Table 5 puts F1 scores from different datasets and tasks side by side (0.21 on PrimeVul to 0.99 on a custom Solidity set) (p. 18). These numbers are not comparable, and the "F1 near 0.9" conclusion (Finding V, p. 19) leans on custom or easier datasets.
- [I] No LLM-vs-SAST or LLM-vs-DL synthesis, despite the motivation in the abstract that traditional tools have high false-positive rates (p. 1). The claim that LLMs "typically assist static analysis tools" (p. 20) is a characterisation, not a quantified comparison.
- [I] Includes smart-contract (Solidity) studies (p. 4), which our project and `kaniewski2026systematic` treat as a separate domain. Corpus shares are therefore not directly comparable with Kaniewski's.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): selection is unsystematic and venue-anchored, and no quality filter is applied (p. 3–4). Preprint share not reported. The survey itself warns that primary studies suffer from data leakage that inflates their metrics (p. 14, p. 25).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): the corpus covers 2019–2024 and is C/C++-heavy (50%) (p. 11). It includes Solidity (p. 4).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): percentages such as ">95% of studies report that code complexity…" (p. 22) and "100% of recent studies" adopting CoT for models above 10B (p. 18) are given without denominators or a coding scheme.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable; F1 values are listed, not pooled.
- Reproducibility: the paper list is on GitHub (p. 1). The search protocol and extraction data are not reported.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Move beyond snippet classification to real-world problems (p. 20–22):
    - full-scale and incremental (commit-level) detection
    - vulnerability reproduction via fuzzers/PoCs, to reduce false positives
    - repair validated by tests
    - CWE-specific detection
    - classification and severity assessment
  - Represent vulnerability semantics better (p. 22–23):
    - let LLMs explore repository code dynamically
    - optimised AST/CFG/DFG representations
    - specialised agents
    - external tools and RAG
  - Address intrinsic LLM limits (p. 24):
    - fine-tune frontier LLMs
    - vulnerability-specific and repository-adaptive fine-tuning
    - ensembles to reduce false positives
    - domain-adaptive pre-training
    - adaptive/continual learning
  - Datasets (p. 25):
    - accurate labels, minimal leakage (obfuscation, synthesis, updated datasets) and rich repository-level annotations
    - small, verified, community-maintained test sets
    - augmentation for long-tail vulnerability types
  - Improve neuro-symbolic (static analysis + LLM) approaches: taint propagation modelling, efficient reasoning, cross-language adaptation (p. 3).
- Suggested by us [I]: none of the directions asks for controlled head-to-head comparisons of LLMs with SAST or DL detectors on the same leakage-controlled benchmark. That absence is directly relevant to our RQ1/RQ5 gap analysis (pending a novelty check).

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (dataset catalogue, granularity, leakage, metric usage), RQ3 (LLM-assisted static analysis and neuro-symbolic directions, qualitative only), RQ4 (language focus, memory vs logic vulnerabilities, CWE variation), RQ5 (challenges and directions).
- How it informs our work [I]: a peer-reviewed (CSUR) but methodologically light survey. Its main value is three things:
  - the dataset catalogue (Table 4);
  - the explicit challenge list (leakage, cross-file context, false positives, robustness, explainability);
  - the qualitative statement that, in practice, LLMs mostly assist static analysis rather than replace it.

  Cite its numbers cautiously, given the internal inconsistencies above, and cite primary studies for any performance figure.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | The survey offers no quantified LLM-vs-SAST/DL comparison; it states that for full-codebase analysis LLMs typically assist static analysis tools or fuzzing rather than performing standalone analysis | 20 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | About 40 studies (83% as stated) evaluate isolated code snippets, where LLM performance exceeds real-world detection performance | 20 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | Existing datasets are narrowly scoped, mislabelled and affected by data leakage that inflates metrics; repository-level datasets are scarce (2 of 42 catalogued) | 3, 13, 25 | A | moderate |
| RQ2 | The same model family scores very differently by benchmark (e.g. CodeBERT 0.099 F1 on PrimeVul vs 0.66 on Choi2017, second-hand) | 19 | A | weak |
| RQ3 | Code-processing techniques (AST/CFG/DFG, RAG, slicing) are used in 41.3% of studies with only modest gains that shrink for cross-file vulnerabilities | 16 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Neuro-symbolic approaches (CodeQL/Bear + LLM) show promise on large projects but need better taint modelling and efficiency | 3 | A | weak |
| RQ4 | 50% of studies target C/C++, 21.1% Java, 11.8% Solidity | 11 | V | weak |
| RQ4 | Memory-related vulnerabilities are detected more accurately than logic vulnerabilities (second-hand claim; the CWE-787 vs CWE-862 example is cited to a mismatched reference [36]) | 3, 22 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Main open challenges: limited problem scope, complex vulnerability semantics and context, LLM robustness and explanation consistency, lack of high-quality datasets | 20–25 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "LLMs typically assist static analysis tools or support fuzzing tasks" (p. 20)

> "Existing datasets are narrowly scoped and have a data leakage problem." (p. 3)

> "Our analysis reveals that 41.3% of studies employed code processing techniques" (p. 16)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 26 body pages read (abstract to conclusion, Tables 1–6, Findings I–IX). The reference list (p. 26–33) was consulted for refs [24], [36], [37], [53], [66] and [121]. Figures 1–12 are images and do not appear in the text layer; their content was taken from the running text.
- Version: arXiv v2 (Feb 2025). The ACM CSUR version (DOI 10.1145/3769082) was not compared and may differ in corpus and time window.
- Overlaps with our corpus: the survey cites IRIS ([66], our `li2024iris`) and Ding et al. ([24], our `ding2025vulnerability`).
- Funding / conflict of interest: not reported.
- Uncertainties: see the inconsistencies in section 9. The 83% denominator and the 72.4% vs 67.1% architecture figures could not be resolved from the text.

# Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead

- Authors: Zhou, Xin; Cao, Sicong; Sun, Xiaobing; Lo, David
- Year / venue: 2025, ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3708522 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3708522
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
- **Version analysed:** arXiv:2404.02525v3 (7 Oct 2024) (p. 1), not the typeset TOSEM version. Numbers and wording may differ slightly from the journal version.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

Convention for this survey: counts about the review's own corpus that appear in its own tables or figures are marked [V]. They are the review's own data, although we cannot re-check the underlying extraction. Anything the survey reports about the results of individual primary studies is second-hand and marked [A], never [V].

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Provide the first systematic literature review focused on how LLMs are used for source-code vulnerability detection **and** repair, identify limitations of existing studies and propose a research roadmap (p. 1, p. 2).
- [A] The authors position it against earlier reviews that covered ML/DL broadly (to 2016, 2020, May 2022) or covered LLMs for SE in general without detailing vulnerability tasks (p. 3).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: What LLMs have been used for vulnerability detection and repair? (p. 5)
- RQ2: How are LLMs adapted for vulnerability detection? (p. 5)
- RQ3: How are LLMs adapted for vulnerability repair? (p. 5)
- RQ4: What are the characteristics of datasets and deployment strategies in these studies? (p. 5)
- No hypotheses; descriptive review.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: SLR "following the guide by Zhang et al." (p. 5). Two search arms: (a) manual search of 13 conferences (ICSE, ESEC/FSE, ASE, ISSTA, CCS, S&P, USENIX Security, NDSS, AAAI, IJCAI, ICML, NIPS, ICLR) and 4 journals (TOSEM, TSE, TDSC, TIFS), yielding 35 papers; (b) automated search of 7 databases yielding 1,500 records, with the search string derived from the manually found papers (p. 5; Fig. 2, p. 4). Then multi-phase screening, quality assessment and forward/backward snowballing (p. 6–7).
- Approach / model / intervention: descriptive classification (taxonomy) of LLMs (encoder-only, encoder-decoder, decoder-only, following Pan et al.) and of adaptation techniques: fine-tuning (data-centric, combination with program analysis, LLM + other DL modules, domain-specific pre-training, causal learning), prompt engineering (zero-/few-shot) and retrieval augmentation (p. 3–4, p. 9–14; Fig. 1, p. 2).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable (review). The review does **not** compare LLM approaches with SAST tools or non-LLM DL detectors. Studies using only GNN/RNN models were explicitly excluded (p. 6).
- Inclusion criteria [A]: English; full text accessible; peer-reviewed full paper in a conference or journal (arXiv preprints from 2023–2024 kept subject to a quality check); uses LLM techniques for source-code vulnerability detection or repair (p. 5).
- Exclusion criteria [A]: fewer than 5 pages; books, keynotes, technical reports, theses, tool demos, editorials; literature reviews and surveys; duplicates or similar studies by the same authors; no LLM use (e.g. GNN only); LLM mentioned only as future work; not source-code detection/repair (binary code, protocols and network excluded) (p. 5–6).
- Quality assessment [A]: five criteria, QAC1–QAC5 (prestigious venue; contribution; clear workflow/implementation; clear experiment details; findings support the claims). Each is scored 0–3, and studies need a total of at least 12 (80%) to be included. Unpublished preprints score 0 on the venue criterion but are kept if they still reach 12 (p. 6).
- Number of reviewers, independent screening, conflict resolution and inter-rater agreement: not reported.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): manual venue search plus IEEE Xplore (197), ACM DL (285), SpringerLink (266), Wiley (205), Web of Science (237), ScienceDirect (220), arXiv (90) [V] (Fig. 2, p. 4).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 58 primary studies [V] (p. 1, p. 7). Selection flow [V] (Fig. 2, p. 4; p. 6–7):
  - 1,535 records
  - 1,387 after the page filter
  - 1,332 after de-duplication
  - 212 after venue/title/abstract screening
  - 82 after full-text screening
  - 42 after quality assessment (37 published + 5 preprints)
  - 58 final, after adding 16 papers from snowballing (83 snowballing candidates)

  The abstract reports 43 published + 15 preprints (p. 1). Table 2 lists 40 detection studies (p. 10) and Table 3 lists 19 repair studies (p. 16) [V].
- Time window: January 2018 – March 2024 (p. 5). The earliest included study is from 2021, and 2024 accounts for 46.6% of studies [V] (p. 7).
- Sampling / selection method: see section 3. Snowballing is described as "lightweight" (p. 7).
- Data availability: search keywords are in an online appendix (Google Doc) (p. 5, ref [8]). Extraction sheet and per-study QA scores: not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, tools: the data extraction and analysis section reports only the distribution of studies by year and venue (p. 7). The extraction form is not reported beyond the fields visible in Tables 2–3: LLM size, adaptation technique, input granularity, data labelling, user interaction and workflow integration (p. 10, p. 16).
- Code availability: not applicable; the online appendix covers keywords only (p. 5).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: frequency counts and percentages of LLM usage (92 LLM usages in detection, 45 in repair) and of adaptation techniques (p. 7–9, p. 14, p. 17). The review does not aggregate the precision, recall or F1 reported by primary studies.
- Statistical testing: none (descriptive review); not reported.

## 7. Key findings
1. Encoder-only LLMs dominate detection. CodeBERT accounts for 26.1% (24/92) of LLM usages and GPT-3.5 for 9.8% (9/92). By architecture: encoder-only 47.8% (44/92), decoder-only 23.9% (22/92), encoder-decoder 9.8% (9/92), commercial with undisclosed architecture 18.5% (17/92) — [V] (p. 7–8)
2. Detection adaptation: fine-tuning ≈73%, prompt engineering ≈17%, retrieval augmentation ≈10% of studies — [V] (p. 9, p. 14). Repair: fine-tuning ≈63%, prompting ≈37% — [V] (p. 14, p. 17)
3. Most detection studies work at function level. Only 7 address line level, none address class level, and one works at repo level ([130], which is our `zhou2024comparison`) — [V] (p. 17–18)
4. Detection datasets mostly use heuristic labels: functions changed by vulnerability-fixing commits are labelled vulnerable in their pre-fix version, and other functions are labelled clean. Prior work has shown these labels to be noisy — [A] (p. 18)
5. Repair datasets mostly lack test cases. The two studies that have them evaluate only 42 and 12 samples — [A] (p. 18)
6. None of the reviewed studies is integrated into developer workflows; all are evaluated offline on static historical data. Only one detection study ([113]) produces explanations for developers — [V] (Tables 2–3; p. 19)
7. The only LLM-vs-SAST evidence comes from [130]: SAST tools reach low detection rates with relatively few false positives, while LLMs detect more vulnerabilities but have high false-positive rates. This is second-hand, from a study by the same first and last authors — [A] (p. 22)
8. The best reported state of the art is cited as 67.6% accuracy for detection and 20% for repair (refs [56], [128]) — [A], second-hand (p. 20–21)
9. Cited studies report that LLMs are not robust to data perturbations ([116], [59]). Others report that LLMs struggle with rare CWE types and with inter-procedural or multi-unit vulnerabilities ([51], [84], [128], [129]) — [A] (p. 20–21)

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The only threat to validity discussed is missing relevant studies because of incomplete keywords or varied LLM terminology. It is mitigated by manual venue selection, automated search and snowballing (p. 24).
- [A] Scope: future versions will add vulnerability localisation and assessment (p. 24).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Dated corpus. The search ends in March 2024 (p. 5), before most agentic, repository-level and LLM + SAST hybrid work. Findings such as "encoder-only dominates" may not hold for 2025–2026: `kaniewski2026systematic` and `sheng2025llms` already report decoder-only dominance. Based on the time window and comparison with the other two surveys in this project.
- [I] Very thin evidence on LLM vs SAST. The single repo-level comparison is the authors' own study ([130], Zhou … Lo, 2024; ref list p. 29). The roadmap's statement about SAST-vs-LLM trade-offs is therefore effectively self-citation, not a synthesis.
- [I] No comparison with non-LLM DL detectors. GNN/RNN-only studies are excluded (p. 6), so the review cannot answer whether LLMs beat DL detectors.
- [I] The quality assessment uses "published in a prestigious venue" (QAC1) as a criterion (p. 6). This mixes venue prestige with methodological quality and structurally penalises preprints.
- [I] Gaps in process transparency: the number of screeners, their agreement and the per-study QA scores are not reported, and the search string is only in an external Google Doc (p. 5).
- [I] Minor internal inconsistencies:
  - The RQ3 answer says "three commonly used techniques" but lists two (p. 17).
  - Limitation 2 opens with "For vulnerability repair" while discussing detection label noise (p. 19).
  - By our count, Tables 2 and 3 contain 57 unique study references (Fu et al. [27] and [29] appear in both), versus 58 stated.

  None of these changes the main conclusions.
- [I] Repair is half of the scope, so detection-specific depth (metrics, benchmarks, CWE coverage) is limited.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): selection could be biased by the venue-first strategy and the prestige-weighted QA. Whether one or several people screened each paper is not reported. The review itself flags contamination of LLM pre-training corpora as a concern for primary studies (p. 20).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): the corpus covers Jan 2018–Mar 2024 and source code only, no binaries (p. 5–6). It is dominated by function-level studies (Table 2, p. 10).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): the technique shares (≈73/17/10%) are given without a stated denominator (p. 9). The classification of studies into categories is not validated.
- Statistical conclusion: not applicable (no quantitative synthesis).
- Reproducibility: keywords are in an online appendix (p. 5). Extraction data and QA scores are not released (not reported).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - Curate a smaller, manually verified, living high-quality test set for vulnerability detection, e.g. by combining manually checked samples from several studies (p. 22).
  - Repository-level detection and repair using long-context LLMs, extending the initial repo-level SAST-vs-LLM comparison (p. 22).
  - Open-source LLMs customised for vulnerability data (p. 22).
  - LLM usages not yet explored: agents, external tool use, advanced RAG (iterative, recursive, adaptive) (p. 22–23).
  - Deployment-ready features: developer interaction, explanations, IDE/VCS integration (p. 23).
  - Benchmarks with no overlap with LLM pre-training corpora, to avoid data contamination (p. 20).
  - Handling complex vulnerabilities: inter-procedural, rare CWE types, vulnerabilities spanning multiple code units (p. 20).
  - Vision for 2030: line- to repo-level detection and repair, evaluated on an expert-annotated benchmark (p. 23).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - Check whether the agent, tool-use and repo-level directions proposed here have since been realised. Our corpus contains `guo2025repoaudit`, `li2024iris`, `yildiz2025benchmarking` and `li2026llm`.
  - Check whether the SAST-vs-LLM trade-off reported by `zhou2024comparison` (higher detection for LLMs, but more false positives) replicates in independent studies.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (dataset labelling, granularity, contamination) and RQ5 (limitations and roadmap). Marginally RQ1 (one second-hand SAST-vs-LLM statement) and RQ4 (rare CWEs, inter-procedural vulnerabilities).
- How it informs our work [I]: a peer-reviewed (TOSEM) baseline of the field up to March 2024. It mainly shows two things:
  - As of early 2024, head-to-head SAST-vs-LLM evidence was almost absent.
  - Dataset quality, small input granularity and missing workflow integration were already named as key gaps.

  Its LLM-vs-SAST statement should be cited to the primary study `zhou2024comparison`, not to this survey.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Only one study in the 58-study corpus compares LLMs with SAST tools (repo level). It reports that SAST tools have low detection rates with few false positives, while LLMs detect more but with high false-positive rates. Second-hand, and the study is the survey authors' own | 18, 22 | A | weak |
| RQ2 | Most LLM detection studies work at function level (7 at line level, 0 at class level, 1 at repo level) | 17–18 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Detection datasets mostly use heuristic labels from vulnerability-fixing commits, which prior work has shown to be noisy | 18 | A | moderate |
| RQ2 | Benchmarks may overlap with LLM pre-training corpora (data contamination); contamination-free benchmarks are recommended | 20 | A | moderate |
| RQ4 | LLMs reportedly struggle more with less frequent CWE types and with inter-procedural and multi-unit vulnerabilities | 20 | A | weak |
| RQ5 | Building a high-quality vulnerability detection benchmark remains an open challenge; a curated, living, manually verified test set is proposed | 19, 22 | A | moderate |
| RQ5 | None of the 58 studies is integrated into developer workflows, and almost none supports developer interaction or explanations | 19 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Directions still under-explored as of Mar 2024: repo-level detection, LLM agents, external tool use, LLMs customised for vulnerabilities | 22–23 | A | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "Constructing a high-quality vulnerability detection benchmark remains an open challenge to date." (p. 19)

> "all studies in our review are not integrated into developers’ workflows and tools but are evaluated only offline using static and historical data" (p. 19)

> "SAST tools achieve low vulnerability detection rates with relatively low false positives, whereas LLMs can detect more vulnerabilities but tend to suffer from high false positive rates" (p. 22)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 24 body pages read (abstract to conclusion, Tables 1–3, Figs. 1–8). The reference list (p. 24–30) was consulted for refs [8], [56], [84] and [128]–[130]. Figures 2–8 are partly garbled in the text layer, so counts were taken from the running text where both exist.
- Version: arXiv v3 (Oct 2024). The published TOSEM version (DOI 10.1145/3708522) was not compared.
- Uncertainties:
  - The denominators of the 73/17/10% technique shares are not stated.
  - The abstract's split of 43 published + 15 preprints is not reconciled with the 37 + 5 papers after QA plus 16 snowballed papers.
- Funding / conflict of interest: funded by the National Research Foundation, Singapore (p. 24). The only SAST-vs-LLM evidence in the survey is the authors' own work ([130]).
